study.title: NPV in simple English
study.section: Performing Financial Analyses → Net Present Value (NPV)
study.simple: NPV is the value today of all project benefits minus the value today of all project costs. Use the full discounting formula for each year rather than multiplying by rounded two-decimal factors.
steps: Project benefits are R0; R110 000; R135 000; R160 000; R185 000.
Exact discounted costs total R430 111,02 and exact discounted benefits total R458 138,11.
study.remember: Positive NPV means the discounted benefits are greater than the discounted costs.

keyTerms.meaning: The value gained or lost after future project benefits and costs are converted into today's money; NPV = discounted benefits minus discounted costs.
The annual percentage used to reduce future cash amounts to what they are worth today; future money is not treated as identical to money now.
A multiplier used to express money from a future year in today's value. Formula: 1 / (1 + rate)^year.

study.example: For Year 2, the benefit is R135 000 / 1.10² = R111 570,25. Do the same for each future benefit and cost, then subtract the two totals.
study.pitfall: The original source/key reported R27 953 because it used rounded discount factors. That value is kept only as source metadata and is no longer offered as a selectable answer. Use the full 10% discounting formula.

questions.text: A project’s net profit is calculated by:
options: Adding total cash inflows to the initial investment
Deducting total expenses from total income
Adding total expenses to the initial investment
Deducting total cash inflows from total cash outflows
questions.correctAnswer: Deducting total expenses from total income

study.title: Net profit
study.simple: Net profit is simply what is left after all project expenses are removed from all project income.
steps: Net profit = total income − total expenses.
study.remember: Income minus expenses. If expenses are bigger, the result is a loss.

keyTerms.meaning: Total income minus total project expenses. It is money, not a percentage.
Total money earned or received by a project before its costs are subtracted.
Money used or spent to deliver and operate the project.

study.example: Income R140 000 minus expenses R90 000 leaves net profit R50 000.
study.pitfall: Revenue is the money received; profit is what remains after expenses are taken away.

questions.explanation:
Net profit is simply what is left after all project expenses are removed from all project income.

How to reach the marked answer: Add all income or revenue. Add all expenses or costs. Net profit = total income − total expenses.

Example: Income R140 000 minus expenses R90 000 leaves net profit R50 000.

Student note: Revenue is the money received; profit is what remains after expenses are taken away.

study.title: Early and late times
study.section: Critical Path Method → Forward and Backward Pass
study.simple: The forward pass gives the earliest times an activity can happen. The backward pass gives the latest times it can happen without delaying the project.
study.remember: Forward: EF = ES + duration. Backward: LS = LF − duration.

Late Start / Late Finish: the latest allowed start and finish calculated by the backward pass without delaying project completion.

study.example: For a two-day activity with ES 3, EF = 3 + 2 = 5; if LF is 10, LS = 10 - 2 = 8.

The forward pass gives the earliest times an activity can happen. The backward pass gives the latest times it can happen without delaying the project.

Example: For a two-day activity with ES 3, EF = 3 + 2 = 5; if LF is 10, LS = 10 - 2 = 8.

questions.text: You must choose between embarking on Project Y or Project Z. Return on investment (ROI) is one of the factors you are taking into account to inform your decision. Apply the annualised ROI formula to calculate the ROI of Project Z.

study.title: Annualised ROI
study.simple: Annualised ROI spreads the total ROI across the number of project years so you can compare projects on a yearly basis.
study.remember: Annualised ROI = total ROI divided by the number of years when the assessment uses this simple annualising method.

keyTerms.meaning: The return compared with the cost of investing, commonly shown as a percentage: (benefits minus costs) / costs × 100.
An average return expressed per year. This assessment divides simple total ROI by the four project years.

study.example: Project Z receives R310 000 in four years against R275 000 invested: total ROI = R35 000 / R275 000 ≈ 12.73%; average per year ≈ 3.18%.
study.pitfall: This question uses simple annualising (total ROI / four years). It is not a compound annual growth rate.

questions.explanation:
Annualised ROI spreads the total ROI across the number of project years so you can compare projects on a yearly basis.

How to reach the marked answer: Project Z total inflow = 70 000 + 75 000 + 80 000 + 85 000 = R310 000. Profit = 310 000 − 275 000 = R35 000. Total ROI = 35 000 / 275 000 ≈ 12.73%. Annualised over 4 years: 12.73% / 4 ≈ 3.18%.

Example: Project Z receives R310 000 in four years against R275 000 invested: total ROI = R35 000 / R275 000 ≈ 12.73%; average per year ≈ 3.18%.

Student note: This question uses simple annualising (total ROI / four years). It is not a compound annual growth rate.
